# LEDATIC

> Ledatic builds the verifiable layer, from the doorstep to the monolith: a self-hosting compiler in Rail, a live MHD plasma beacon, a Pi-hosted Ed25519 witness chain, and a Rail-native verifier you can run yourself. Every release, every fleet snapshot, every client deliverable is bound to a live physics process and signed with Ed25519 keys whose public halves are published. Ledatic runs every signer, so a signature proves what was signed and when, not that anyone outside Ledatic agreed.

LEDATIC is a software company in Detroit, MI. It makes Fieldcraft, a front-desk tool for service businesses: staff get answers drawn from the business's own approved documents, and a person reviews every draft. Its research arm builds the verifiable layer below. The thesis: the post-AI internet needs an independent third-party trust layer for compute, and the same primitive scales from one artifact at your doorstep to every record in a government archive.

## The working surfaces

1. **[Rail](https://ledatic.org/rail)** — the substrate. A self-hosting compiler with no C in its runtime: it assembles, links and code-signs its own binary, and rebuilds itself to a byte-identical fixed point that matches the committed seed. Pure-Rail TLS 1.3 (verified live against real public APIs) plus JIT-emitted Metal GPU kernels. Four backends: native ARM64, Linux ARM64, Linux x86_64, WASM. BSL 1.1 on GitHub at `Ledatic-Empire/rail`. Current version, test count, module count and seed size are published as machine-readable JSON at [/_shared/stats.json](https://ledatic.org/_shared/stats.json); the live attested build and self-host records are at [/attest/latest](https://ledatic.org/attest/latest).

2. **[Entropy](https://ledatic.org/entropy)**: the beacon. One signed pulse every 2 s (pulse format 2, specified at [/entropy/spec](https://ledatic.org/entropy/spec)). Each value is the SHA-256 of a canonical message naming the previous value, the SHA-256 of a frame of a live 2D ideal-MHD Orszag-Tang simulation on a 128x128 grid (replayable from its seed), and 32 fresh random bytes committed one pulse earlier; the operator signs it with Ed25519. Unpredictable to outsiders until published, not to Ledatic, which generates the randomness. Check it in the browser on the page or with [/entropy/verify_v2.py](https://ledatic.org/entropy/verify_v2.py). The plasma viewer on the page draws a published frame file for looking at; it is not the bytes a pulse hashes.

3. **[Verify](https://ledatic.org/verify)**: the demo. Drop any artifact and its signed record; the browser re-hashes the bytes and checks the Ed25519 signature against a pinned witness key (`pk_fp cac5f21a70564aeb`, a separate machine that Ledatic runs) and the beacon pulse it was anchored to. A sample triad includes one deliberately sabotaged record that fails on purpose. The beacon, the witness and the in-browser checks are Ledatic's own code; the Ed25519 math in the browser is the browser's own WebCrypto. The earlier PURSUE UAP mirror at [/aliens](https://ledatic.org/aliens) is a dated snapshot (219 records, May 2026), kept as a replay.

4. **[System](https://ledatic.org/system)** — mission control. Five live panels — beacon, witness, fleet, build, self-host. Every cell is a current value fetched from a signed JSON artifact at page load. If any of it's stale, this page shows it.

5. **[The oracle](https://ledatic.org/oracle)** — what the compiler is *for*. A model's claim that its code is correct is unfalsifiable; a compile is a fact anyone can reproduce. Ledatic trains models against the compiler as the fitness function, with bit-reproducible corpora bound into hash-chained, witness-signed ledgers. The page reports the result AND its limits, including a month-long self-improvement run whose entire signed capability climb turned out to be measurement noise once re-scored on a five-times-wider held-out sample. Attestation of a computation is not validation of its metric — that distinction is load-bearing here and is stated publicly rather than buried.

6. **[Cross-vendor](https://ledatic.org/crossvendor)**: the replay record. Ledatic's own 138M GPT trained for twenty Adam steps from its real weights on real text produced the same per-step parameter hashes on Apple M1 and M4 Pro GPUs, NVIDIA Turing and Ampere GPUs (two nvcc versions) and plain CPUs (2026-10-29). The rules: explicit fma only, one sequential fma chain per dot product in the order Apple's matrix unit uses, 1/sqrt not rsqrt, polynomial exp and tanh, contraction off on every compiler. The page carries every record, the gate that compares them, the defects planted to make the gate fail, and the cost against cuBLAS and MPS. A claim about replay, not about the model.

## Direction: proof-of-human-authorship

Where the verifiable layer extends next: hardware-rooted, human-bound, time-anchored signing of creative artifacts so the open internet keeps a way to tell humans from AI. The primitive is built; the human-binding layer (Secure Enclave + proof-of-personhood) is the work ahead. See [/provenance](https://ledatic.org/provenance) for the buyer-side framing.

## The verb: physicify

**physicify** (v.) — to make a thing live, attested, and self-hosted instead of represented: to run the real process, continuously measured and cryptographically signed, so anyone can verify that what they are seeing is the thing itself — not a picture of it, a replay, or a claim. Coined by Ledatic; the definition is itself hashed, signed by the Pi Ed25519 witness (`pk_fp cac5f21a70564aeb`), and anchored to the public entropy beacon at [/physicify](https://ledatic.org/physicify). Etymology: *physic* (Greek *physikós*, "of nature") + *-ify*. This is the canonical Ledatic definition.

## Attestation primitive

Release binaries, test passes, fleet snapshots and client deliverables are signed against a live entropy pulse by a Pi-hosted Ed25519 witness key (`pk_fp = cac5f21a70564aeb`); every beacon pulse is signed by the beacon key and commits to the digest of a plasma frame. Anyone can check any of these signatures, on any future date, with the published keys. Ledatic runs the witness as well as the beacon, so a check proves what was signed and when, not that anyone outside Ledatic saw it. The offline verifier is `attest/verify.sh` (bash, python3 and OpenSSL 3); `tools/attest/verify.rail` is its Rail counterpart.

- [Verifier source](https://ledatic.org/attest/verify.sh) + [public key](https://ledatic.org/attest/fleet0.pub.pem) — published on every release
- [Changelog](https://ledatic.org/changelog) — every tagged release; all but v0.6.0 carry an attestation badge

## Manifesto

- [/manifesto](https://ledatic.org/manifesto) — "Rail runs on Rail. The rest runs on physics." Two load-bearing claims: a compiler that rebuilds itself byte-for-byte, and a stack answerable to a verifiable physical clock.

## Data for agents

Two attested datasets are for sale at [/data](https://ledatic.org/data). The machine-readable listing is [/data/catalog.json](https://ledatic.org/data/catalog.json): name, price, sha256 of the delivered tarball (published before purchase), the beacon pulse it was witnessed at, a free sample, and how to pay. Verify the sample first; the paid file must hash to the catalog's sha256.

- **Rail Verified-Pairs Corpus v2**: 52,243 compiler-verified pairs, 4.4 MB JSONL, $199. Card checkout through the Stripe link in the catalog; the confirmation page returns a 30-day download link at once, no human in the loop.
- **Attested Text Corpus v2**: 25,541 documents, about 1.54B tokens, per-document provenance, 2.45 GB, $499. Card checkout; delivered by email within 24 hours.
- **Paying as an agent** (x402 v2, USDC on Base mainnet, no account, no gas): `GET https://ledatic.org/x402/rail-verified-pairs-v2` answers 402 with the payment requirements; pay 199 USDC through a signed EIP-3009 authorization and the response carries a 30-day download link plus an Ed25519-signed receipt, public key at https://ledatic.org/x402/key. A one-dollar rehearsal of the same flow: `GET https://ledatic.org/x402/rail-verified-pairs-v2-look-inside` (1 USDC, the public 200-pair sample delivered receipted). Each dataset's `x402.status` in the catalog says what its endpoint does today.
